title: Helping At-Risk Customers
summary: How do you help at-risk customers? Confirm what changed, check the account history and open commitments, then choose new help, follow-through, or no outreach.
body_markdown:
## TL;dr


At-risk customers need a response that fits what actually changed, and the signal that flagged them rarely says enough to choose one. Before anyone writes to the customer, confirm the change, read the account's history, and check what your team has already agreed to do. That review usually points to one of three responses: new help aimed at the specific problem, follow-through on work already promised, or no outreach at all.


Outlit's churn agent runs that investigation from customer memory and proposes the response. The account owner approves what reaches the customer, and discounts stay a person's decision.


## When does the same risk signal need different responses?


Most CS teams have some way to see risk. The weak point is the step after, when a signal triggers the save motion attached to it. Usage dropped, so send the check-in. The champion's title changed, so book the executive call. The playbook runs whether or not the account history already explains the change.


That's how a customer who announced a seasonal pause gets three re-engagement emails. Each one makes sense in isolation. Together they tell the customer that nobody read the thread.


Treat the signal as a reason to look. Three questions decide what happens next:


1. Is the change confirmed? A title change, a bounced email, or a quiet inbox suggests a departure. An auto-reply saying the person has left, or the customer telling you directly, confirms one.
2. Does the history explain it? A product incident, a paused implementation, a seasonal cycle, or a decision the customer already shared changes what a drop means. Missing product tracking means usage is unknown, which is different from usage falling to zero.
3. What is already in motion? An open support fix, an agreed pause, or a commitment made on the last call may already be the response. Then the job is making sure that work happens.


## How does context change the response?


The three situations below are illustrative. The accounts are invented, and each one is built around a type of risk Outlit's churn agent is designed to work. They show how the decision changes, not customer results.


### The champion leaves


Your champion's auto-reply says they've left the company. Without something that explicit, the owner confirms the departure before anyone writes to the customer about it.


If last month's call notes name the person taking over the rollout, the first note goes to them within a day or two: an introduction from the owner and a pointer to the open work. If nobody is named, ask the executive sponsor who owns it now, then another contact you already know there.


### A workflow goes quiet


` PostHog` shows one team stopped running its weekly reports two weeks ago. The rest of the account looks normal.


` Pylon` shows that team reported an export bug, and it was fixed last Thursday. The useful message explains the fix and points them back to the report, without reading their activity back to them.


Change the history and the response changes with it. If the call notes record that the team paused reporting during a reorganization, nothing goes out, and the owner checks back after the agreed restart date. If nothing explains the drop, offer help with that specific workflow, then a working session if the first note doesn't land.


### Auto-renew is switched off


` Stripe` shows auto-renew turned off on an annual plan.


A call recorded in` Gong` last month explains it. The customer is consolidating two teams into one workspace, and the CSM agreed to move the second team's data across and not invoice that workspace at renewal. No save email goes out. The owner confirms the migration is scheduled and that billing knows about the promise.


Without that history, the response is a single question to whoever manages the subscription: what changed? Their answer sets the next step, which might be fewer seats, a pause, or a smaller plan. If they ask for a discount, a person decides.


## How do you know the response worked?


Name the recovery evidence before acting, because each situation has its own: a new champion who is active, the dropped workflow running again, auto-renew back on, possibly on a smaller plan. Most of those checks have short windows, measured in weeks or the rest of the subscription term.


Whether the customer is still paying, or back at their usual level of use, two or three months later is a separate and slower result. Track the two apart. The short check tells you whether the response fixed the problem. The longer one tells you whether fixing it mattered.


## Where does Outlit fit?


A CSM can run these checks by hand for a small book. Across hundreds of accounts, the slow part is assembling the history: the auto-reply in` Gmail` , the fix in` Pylon` , the commitment in a call transcript, the subscription change in` Stripe` .


Outlit resolves those records into one customer and keeps customer memory of what the customer raised and what your team agreed. That memory is part of Outlit's[customer context infrastructure](https://www.outlit.ai/blog/what-is-customer-context-infrastructure) . When a risk signal fires, the churn agent reads it alongside billing, contacts, open work, and earlier investigations, then proposes a response. It might be a specific play with its first message drafted for the owner, a request for the owner to confirm a departure or keep a promise, or a decision to leave the customer alone. A proposed play cites the records it relied on.


The owner approves what reaches the customer. Outlit can record the agent's decisions for review before putting work on an owner's list. Availability depends on which signals are enabled for the workspace. When an account enters its renewal cycle, the renewal workflow takes it over; see[how Outlit works a renewal](https://www.outlit.ai/blog/how-to-run-your-renewal-process-with-outlit) .


Take the risk that has come up in your weekly review more than once. Confirm the change if nobody has, then decide whether it needs new help, follow-through on something already agreed, or no outreach. Write down what recovery would look like and when you'll check.
